hook.line: Vale and Hernando have a new hobby: listing everything Tomás has never done. To fight back, you need three things: have you ever, I've never, and not yet.

examples.en: Have you been to Cartagena? (to a friend)

examples.es: Vale ha estado en Cartagena dos veces.
examples.en: Vale has been to Cartagena twice.

examples.es: Todavía no he leído el contrato.
examples.en: I haven't read the contract yet.

examples.es: Mis papás nunca han estado en Colombia.
examples.en: My parents have never been to Colombia.
Have you all been to Medellín?

rule:
English and Spanish build this the same way: a helper verb plus a past form. English says I have been; Spanish says *he estado*.

The helper:
*he*: I have
*has*: you have
*ha*: he, she, you (formal) have
*hemos*: we have
*han*: they, you all have

The past form ends in *-ado* for *-ar* verbs (*estado*, *montado*) and *-ido* for *-er* and *-ir* verbs (*comido*, *vivido*). It never changes. A few are irregular: *hecho* (done, made), *visto* (seen), *dicho* (said), *escrito* (written), *abierto* (opened).

In Colombia it has a narrow job: your life so far, with no date attached (*nunca*, *dos veces*), and things that haven't happened yet (*todavía no*). For something you did at a time, even today, keep the plain past: *Hoy fui al banco*.
smallPrint: Teachers call this the present perfect (*pretérito perfecto*), built from the verb *haber* and a past participle. In Spain it also covers things done today; in Latin America the plain past does that.
soundTip: The *h* is silent, as always in Spanish. *He* sounds like the *e* in *bet*, and *ha* is just *ah*.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick and type the whole sentence: *Nunca ___ montado a caballo.* (*he* or *ha*) I've never ridden a horse.
yourTurn.why: I have is *he*; *ha* is he or she.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick and type the whole sentence: *¿___ estado en Cartagena?* (*Has* or *Ha*) Asking a friend.
yourTurn.why: To a friend, you have is *has*.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick and type the whole sentence: *Todavía no he ___ el contrato.* (*leído* or *leí*) I haven't read the contract yet.
yourTurn.answer: Todavía no he leído el contrato.
yourTurn.why: After *he* comes the form ending in *-ido*, never the plain past.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: We've been to Medellín twice.
yourTurn.answer: Hemos estado en Medellín dos veces.
accept: Hemos estado dos veces en Medellín.

yourTurn.why: *Comer* is an *-er* verb, so its past form is *comido*.

yourTurn.prompt: Ask Don Hernando, politely: Have you been to Cartagena?
yourTurn.why: With *usted*, the helper is *ha*, the same as for he or she.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it about Vale and Hernando: *Nunca he estado en Leticia.*
yourTurn.answer: Vale y Hernando nunca han estado en Leticia.
yourTurn.why: Two people means they, so *he* becomes *han*.

yourTurn.prompt: Turn it into not yet: *Hice el café.*
yourTurn.answer: Todavía no he hecho el café.
yourTurn.why: Not yet takes *todavía no* with *he*, and *hacer* turns into *hecho*.

pitfalls.why: Close. This have isn't *tener*: Spanish uses *he*, *has*, *ha*.
Almost. *He* is only for I; for Vale it's *ha*.
*Hacer* is one of the irregular ones: *hecho*.
In Colombia a finished thing takes the plain past, even today. *He* is for ever, never and not yet.

personal: Write three true lines about your life: a place you've been (*he estado*), something you've never done (*nunca he*), and something you haven't done yet (*todavía no he*).
